The bustle was a framework of steel hoops, petticoats, or padding worn beneath skirts at the rear to create projection and silhouette at the back of a woman's dress. It was dominant in the eighteen seventies through eighties and again briefly in the eighties through nineties. Replacing the all-around volume of the crinoline, the bustle concentrated decorative fabric and shape at the rear, creating one of history's most dramatically angular and impractical silhouettes.

The first bustle era from eighteen sixty-nine to eighteen seventy-six featured a sharp projection from the lower back, creating an almost shelf-like protrusion that shifted the body's center of gravity and required altered posture and movement. Constructed from flexible steel hoops sewn into a petticoat frame worn under the skirt, the rear projection could extend up to twenty-four inches from the body. The second bustle era from eighteen eighty-one to eighteen eighty-nine featured an even more dramatic, nearly vertical projection, sometimes with elaborate flounces and decorative layers creating additional height and volume.

The bustle required altered furniture design entirely. Narrow chairs, carriage seats, and even theater seats had to be modified to accommodate women wearing bustles, as sitting was functionally difficult. The garment was associated with a top-heavy, exaggerated feminine silhouette that contemporary critics considered ugly and ungainly, yet fashion devotees embraced it as the height of modernity. Simplified skirt designs that worked with bustles featured dramatic asymmetry, layered drapery, and elaborate trains that compensated for the rear projection with visual complexity.

The bustle declined rapidly by the eighteen nineties as the Gibson Girl aesthetic and modern fashion movements rejected extreme silhouettes in favor of more natural proportions. In its time, it shares a particular relationship with the crinoline, the earlier garment that distributed volume evenly rather than concentrating it posteriorly, and the corset, the essential companion that exaggerated the S-curve silhouette of the bustle era. The bustle itself became inexorably linked with Victoria, the British queen during both bustle eras, who represented the enduring Victorian commitment to extreme fashion.
